4.text: The human husband of Tiluˊwg̣i was an undersized fellow, shorter than

5.text: his “wife” by at least half a head. He was nevertheless healthy and strong,

6.text: a good wrestler and runner, and altogether a normal, well-balanced person.

7.text: He was a cousin of Tiluˊwg̣i, as generally the transformed shamans prefer to

8.text: choose a husband from among their nearest relatives.

9.text: The division of labor between the two followed, of course, the usual

10.text: rules. In the evening, Yaˊtirg̣ɪn would sit idly within the inner room, while

11.text: Tiluˊwg̣i busied himself outside with the hearth and the supper. Yaˊtirg̣ɪn,

12.text: received the best pieces of meat, and the transformed “wife,” according to

13.text: custom, had to be content with scraps and bones. In the more serious affairs

14.text: of life, the voice of the “wife” was, however, dominant.

15.text: I heard also from their neighbors a curious story, that one time, when

16.text: Yaˊtirg̣ɪn was angry at something and wanted to chastise his giant wife, the

17.text: latter suddenly gave him so powerful a kick that it sent him head foremost

18.text: from their common sleeping-room. This proves that the femininity of Tiluˊwg̣i

20.text: The transformation in Tiluˊwg̣i began in his very early youth, after a

21.text: protracted illness from which he freed himself by the song and the drum.

22.text: He gave a shamanistic seance in my presence, which had no peculiar features,

23.text: except that the keˊlᴇ-husband often appeared and talked to the public, extolling

24.text: the shaman. In the very beginning, Tiluˊwg̣i called him and asked him to

25.text: mend the drum, which, as he pretended, had not the proper ring.¹ We

26.text: heard the keˊlᴇ-husband blow with great force over the cover of the drum,

27.text: after which its sound at once improved.

28.text: Another shaman of transformed sex was Eˊčhuk, whom I met at the

29.text: Anui fair. He was a person of about forty, tall and strong, of rather

30.text: indecent behavior and strongly peppered talk. He boasted even that he had

31.text: been able to bear two sons from his own body, through the assistance of

33.text: Keeˊᵋulin, of the village of Aˊčon, was an old man of sixty, a widower,

34.text: whose wife had borne him several children. At the same time the people

35.text: asserted that he had a male lover with whom he had lived for more than

36.text: twenty years. Now his male lover was also dead, so he was doubly widowed.

37.text: He wore female dress, but his face was covered with stubs of gray beard,

38.text: and his head was too bald to leave enough hair to be arranged in braids.

39.text: He was quite poor, and even the shamanistic power had gone from him to

40.text: a considerable degree. He was said, however, to have a new lover, —

41.text: another old man who lived in the same house with him.
